# Blackbaud, Inc. (BLKB) — Interrogator Forensic Dossier

*Vertical SaaS · Social-impact sector software · Signal: deep_value · Price $27.90 · P/FCF 5.2x*

Source transcripts: Q1-2025 (2025-04-30), Q2-2025 (2025-07-30), Q4/FY-2025 (2026-02-10). *Note: the bundle includes a misfiled Q3-2025 transcript that is actually **Bausch + Lomb's** call (Brent Saunders / Miebo / IOLs) — it is NOT Blackbaud and is disregarded for this dossier.* Financials per screener scan (FY-2025) plus FMP TTM/latest-quarter (2026-03-31) and live balance-sheet corrections.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story across the available Blackbaud calls is remarkably **consistent and on-message** — almost to a fault. The through-line is "**Rule of 40 → Rule of 45 by 2030**," a profitable-growth efficiency narrative that management has executed against and, by FY-2025, **beat two years ahead of plan** ("We accomplished our goal of becoming a Rule of 40 company 2 years ahead of plan," Q4-2025).

The arc has three stacked layers, each added without dropping the prior:

1. **Operational rightsizing (the base case, present since Q1-2025):** three-year contract migration begun in 2023 for "nearly two-thirds of our revenue base," exit of owned data centers ("only two of our own data centers remaining"), office-lease rationalization, vendor renegotiation. This is a margin-and-visibility story, and it is the most credible layer.
2. **Capital return (the headline shareholder pitch):** "in 2024, the company bought back 10% of the common stock outstanding… 11%" incl. net-share-settle (Q1-2025); 4.2% repurchased by end of Q1-2025; a stated plan to buy "3% to 5%" in 2025, later escalated in the FY-2025 aspirational framework to "**50% of free cash flow** to repurchases through 2030." Buyback is explicitly "**our top priority from a capital strategy standpoint**" (Q4-2025).
3. **AI / Agentic optionality (the new growth layer, ramping Q2→Q4-2025):** introduced as "embedded AI" and "Blackbaud Copilot" (Q1-2025), expanded to "AI Everywhere" and a "full Agentic offering" launching at bbcon-October (Q2-2025), and crystallized into "**Blackbaud Agents for Good**" / a "**fundraising Development Agent**" as a "**new revenue line**" by Q4-2025.

What is notable is what is **emphasized late vs early**: the **"data moat"** language ("We have a data moat… This cannot be commoditized," Q4-2025) is a clear defensive escalation in response to the existential question management itself posed — "**Will AI be beneficial to system of record vertical software firms like Blackbaud or detrimental.**" That the CEO felt compelled to "address head on the big question our industry is facing" is the single most important tonal tell in the bundle: the AI optionality is being marketed partly to **inoculate against an AI-disruption bear case**, not purely as upside.

Quietly absent from the narrative: any acknowledgment of the **share-price collapse** (the stock is down ~46% vs its 200-day SMA and sits 3% off its 52-week low), the **negative ROE/ROIC**, the **$1.14B net debt load**, or the **rejected Clearlake take-private bids** ($71 in 2023, $80 in 2024). Management speaks as if the equity is healthy; the tape says otherwise.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Trajectory: STABLE-to-rising, but with a defensive undertone introduced late.**

Simultaneously the long-term aspirational framework (Rule of 45, 50%-of-FCF buyback) is the most specific multi-year guidance given, which cuts the other way (confidence to commit to dated targets).

The shift from "growth/investment" to a blend of "**efficiency + moat-defense**" language between Q2 and Q4 is the meaningful directional move. There is no panic — but there is a clear awareness that the equity market is pricing an existential AI risk that management feels obligated to refute.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: MEDIUM-HIGH on operations, MEDIUM on the equity story.**

- The screener records a **5/6 quarter beat rate (83%)** on EPS — corroborated by the public record (Q1-2026, reported April 2026, again beat on revenue while narrowly missing the Street's EPS by guiding conservatively). This is a **management team that under-promises on the consensus line and delivers operationally.**

The operational guidance is reliable; the **value-creation guidance has not been delivered to shareholders** despite operational delivery — a classic "good business, broken stock" disconnect.

**Score: Medium-High (operational delivery is genuinely strong; the disconnect is between delivery and the share price, which management does not address).**

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Analysts (Koji Ikeda/BofA, Kirk Materne/Evercore, Rob Oliver/Baird, Parker Lane & Matthew Kikkert/Stifel) consistently pushed on three areas:

1. **AI monetization — the central, recurring pressure point.** Across all three calls analysts asked *how* AI/Agentic gets monetized (fee vs consumption vs up-tier SKU). ## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story across the available Blackbaud calls is remarkably **consistent and on-message** — almost to a fault. 1. **Operational rightsizing (the base case, present since Q1-2025):** three-year contract migration begun in 2023 for "nearly two-thirds of our revenue base," exit of owned data centers ("only two of our own data centers remaining"), office-lease rationalization, vendor renegotiation. bull_thesis:
The bull case is that the market has repriced Blackbaud for a collapse that is not showing up in the numbers, and that three of the loudest warning signals on the screen are measurement artefacts rather than facts about the business. Blackbaud sells the software that non-profits, private schools, universities and corporate giving programmes use to raise and account for money; it has done so for about 45 years. At $34.91 a share on 27 July 2026 the whole company is valued at about $1.60B, against trailing-twelve-month revenue of $1.14B and trailing free cash flow of $292M.

Start with the artefacts, because they are why the stock is here. First, the reported 2.3% revenue decline compares fiscal 2025 to fiscal 2024 and is caused by selling the EVERFI business, not by the base eroding; organic growth was 5.8% in the first quarter of 2025 and 6.8% in the second, and revenue in the first quarter of 2026 was up 3.9% year over year. Second, the negative 1.2% return on invested capital is fiscal 2024, the year the company took roughly $408M of impairment and other charges. On the trailing twelve months Blackbaud earned about $231M of operating profit on roughly $1.18B of invested capital, a mid-teens return. Third, the Altman-Z solvency score of 1.2 that flags distress is arithmetic on a book equity of $34.6M, and that equity is near zero only because the company has parked $1.42B of its own repurchased stock in the treasury account. Interest expense of about $67M a year is covered roughly 4.7 times.

What is left when those come out is a quietly good business. Customer retention runs at 92% to 93%, and roughly two-thirds of revenue now sits under three-year-or-longer contracts, with management noting in the fourth quarter of 2025 that more than 20% of customers have asked to move to four years or longer. Gross margin expanded 160 basis points year over year in the first quarter of 2026, to 59.2%. The quality-of-earnings score is a perfect 9 out of 9. Earnings have beaten expectations in five of the last six quarters, including the most recent print. And the capital return is real and verifiable rather than promised: the fully diluted share count has fallen from 51.68M in the second quarter of 2024 to 46.35M in the first quarter of 2026, down 10.3% in seven quarters and 6.3% in the last year alone, net of all stock compensation. Management has committed half of free cash flow to buybacks through 2030.

The demand argument is better than it looks too. The obvious worry is that government funding cuts damage non-profits and therefore Blackbaud. Management's answer is structural and falsifiable: the software sits in the individual-donor fundraising flow, not in the government grant flow. As Mike Gianoni put it in the first quarter of 2025, when a customer's grant revenue comes under pressure they lean harder on the donation platform, not less. No customer failures have been reported.

Then there is the optionality nobody is paying for. Blackbaud shipped its first agentic artificial-intelligence product, the Fundraising Development Agent, into general availability in the first quarter of 2026, ahead of schedule, priced at what Gianoni described as tens of thousands of dollars a year, with the intent to cross-sell it to thousands of existing customers. On 22 July 2026 the company announced several further agents ahead of its October customer conference. None of this revenue is in the 2026 guidance or in the 2030 targets — management has said so explicitly and repeatedly. The bull does not need it to work; the bull needs only for the existing base to hold while the share count shrinks.

Finally, the selling looks to have been mechanical rather than considered. On 18 June 2026 about 6.9 million shares traded, roughly ten times the surrounding daily average, with the stock near its 52-week low of $25.58. Short interest had risen 30.2% during March to about 5.5% of the shares. A company that has fallen to a $1.6B market value is also being handed from mid-capitalisation mandates to small-capitalisation ones, which is a price-insensitive seller with no matching buyer.

Conditions this case depends on: retention must hold at or near 92% to 93% through the 2026 renewal cohort, which is the first large tranche of the three-year contracts signed from 2023; revenue growth must hold at roughly 4% rather than decaying toward zero; and the buyback must continue at something close to its current pace, which in turn requires that profits do not fall far enough to strain a balance sheet carrying about $1.19B of borrowings.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is that Blackbaud is a slowly decelerating, heavily indebted software company whose management is funding a shrinking share count with borrowed money while telling an artificial-intelligence story it will not put a single dollar behind in guidance — and that the people who know the business best have been selling.

Begin with the insiders, because it is the cleanest signal in the file. Over the measured window there were zero open-market purchases against seven sales totalling 54,801 shares. The chief financial officer sold 6,205 shares — 9% of his entire direct holding, cutting it from 69,074 to 62,869 — in a filing reported on 8 June 2026, with the stock near $27 and within weeks of its low. If the shares were genuinely worth twice the price, that is not the behaviour you would observe.

Second, the growth is genuinely stepping down and management has never acknowledged it. In the first quarter of 2025 the guidance language was mid-single-digit-plus organic growth. By February 2026 the long-term commitment had become 4% to 6%, and the 2026 guide itself came in at roughly 4% to 4.5%. That is the bottom of their own band in year one of a five-year plan. Revenue in the first quarter of 2026 grew 3.9%. For context, the peer comparison supplied for this name puts broad software-industry growth expectations several times higher. A business growing 4% is not being mispriced at a low multiple; it is being priced.

Third, the cash flow is worse than the headline. The $292M of trailing free cash flow adds back about $95M of stock-based compensation — roughly a third of the total and 8.3% of revenue. Expense it properly and owner earnings are about $197M, or $4.28 a share. At $34.91 that is a genuine but far less dramatic yield than the 5.5 times free cash flow the screen advertises.

Fourth, and most dangerous, the balance sheet and the buyback are in tension. Blackbaud carries about $1.19B of borrowings against just $42M of its own cash — the $517M of other current assets on the balance sheet is customer money held in trust, matched by an offsetting obligation, and is not the company's to spend. That is roughly 2.9 times earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation once stock compensation is expensed, or about 3.6 times owner earnings. In the first quarter of 2026 the company drew $64.9M of new borrowings and spent $82.1M repurchasing stock. It is, in part, borrowing to buy back shares. Management has already guided adjusted profits to decline slightly year over year in the second quarter of 2026 to fund artificial-intelligence investment. A levered buyback machine works until earnings pause; earnings are pausing now, into a Federal Reserve whose priced base case is a rate rise by December.

Fifth, the artificial-intelligence question is unresolved and cuts against them. Blackbaud's moat is workflow habit plus a data asset, and management asserts rather than demonstrates that the data 'cannot be commoditized.' Meanwhile the company itself reports using generative coding assistants to cut engineering work 'from days to hours.' The same collapse in the cost of building software that helps Blackbaud also helps anyone building a rival donor database. Retention of 92% to 93% sounds strong until you notice it means one customer in fourteen leaves every year, and the company must grow through that. Salesforce's Nonprofit Cloud is a far larger, better-resourced substitute.

Sixth, the Street is still cutting. Price targets have gone from an eight-target average of $52.50 over the past year, to $41.67 across three in the last quarter, to a single $30.00 target from Stifel on 10 July 2026 — down from $45.00, itself down from $50.00, itself down from $70.00. Target velocity is running at negative 21%. The freshest number on the Street sits below today's price.

What would confirm the bear: any retention figure below 92% at the 2026 renewals; a cut to full-year guidance at the 29 July print; a slowdown or suspension of the buyback; or an agent product that is still described in adjectives rather than in bookings by the October customer conference.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market comes down to a single question for a deeply-discounted name: is the Street pricing terminal decline into a business whose earnings power is actually stable? Here the answer is a qualified yes — the market is wrong on the facts, but less wrong on the direction than the bulls think.

Three specific assumptions embedded in the bearish consensus are factually incorrect, and I can name each one.

First, that Blackbaud's revenue is shrinking. It is not. The 2.3% decline that appears on every screen compares fiscal 2025 to fiscal 2024 and reflects the sale of the EVERFI business. Management flagged the distortion directly on the 30 July 2025 call. The organic base grew 5.8% and 6.8% in the first two quarters of 2025 and 3.9% in the first quarter of 2026. Slow is not the same as shrinking, and the entire value-trap framing depends on conflating them.

Second, that the company destroys capital. The widely-quoted negative 1.2% return on invested capital is fiscal 2024 — the year of roughly $408M of impairment and other charges and a $283M reported loss. On the trailing twelve months Blackbaud generated about $231M of operating profit on roughly $1.18B of invested capital, a mid-teens return that is comfortably above any reasonable cost of capital. The screen is describing a write-off and calling it a business model.

Third, that the balance sheet signals distress. The Altman-Z score of 1.2 is arithmetic on a book equity of $34.6M, and that equity is near zero purely because the company has parked $1.42B of repurchased stock in the treasury account. Retiring a tenth of your shares mechanically erases book equity. Interest is covered about 4.7 times. There is no solvency question here; there is a leverage question, which is different and which I take seriously below.

Where the Street is right and the bulls are wrong, and this is why I am not more aggressive: growth genuinely is decelerating. Guidance moved from mid-single-digit-plus in early 2025 to roughly 4% to 4.5% for 2026, the floor of the company's own 4% to 6% long-term band in year one. And management has excluded every dollar of artificial-intelligence revenue from every published figure — the 2026 guide and the 2030 targets alike — which means the entire narrative centrepiece of the last four earnings calls is unfalsifiable. An investor cannot check it, and neither can I.

So the disagreement is real but bounded. The market is pricing a melting franchise; the evidence says a slow-growing, cash-generative one with a genuine unresolved question about its long-term defensibility. That gap is worth roughly the difference between $34.91 and $44 — not the difference between $34.91 and the old $74.88 high.
forcing_function:
Three things could force the market to change its mind, in descending order of how firmly they are dated.

First and hardest: second-quarter 2026 results on Wednesday 29 July 2026, before the United States market opens — a date the company itself confirmed in a press release on 15 July 2026. This is the moment the 2026 renewal cohort becomes visible and full-year guidance is either reaffirmed or cut. It resolves in two days.

Second: bbcon, the company's annual customer conference in October 2026. Blackbaud teased a broader suite of agentic products on 22 July 2026 explicitly in the run-up to it. The event matters not because a product launch re-rates a stock, but because it is the first natural occasion for artificial-intelligence revenue to move from outside guidance to inside it. Management has drawn that line themselves — everything published so far excludes it, and they describe it as the plus. The moment a number appears, the argument stops being unfalsifiable. That said, this one is soft and non-binding: there is no obligation on the company to quantify anything in October.

Third and most reliable, though it is a mechanism rather than an event: the buyback. Half of free cash flow is committed to repurchases through 2030. At the current price that retires roughly 8% to 9% of the shares a year, which by itself delivers the double-digit earnings-per-share growth management has promised even if revenue only grows 4%. This is the part of the thesis that does not require anyone to change their mind — it simply compounds. Its vulnerability is that it is partly debt-funded, so it is also the first thing to be cut if the second-quarter print goes badly.

What is absent, and worth stating plainly: there is no activist, no strategic review, no announced asset sale and no takeover approach on record. A company at 5.5 times headline free cash flow with a sticky customer base is the archetype of a private-equity target, and Blackbaud rejected an approach at a far higher price several years ago — but nothing is live today, and I am not going to underwrite a bid that does not exist.
valley_of_death:
The risky window here is unusually short and unusually specific: it starts in two days.

The first hazard is the second-quarter print on 29 July 2026, and the problem is not the result — it is the setup. Management has already told the market that adjusted profits will decline slightly year over year this quarter to fund artificial-intelligence investment. Spending up and margins pausing is precisely the message that the current tape has been punishing: in the same reporting season Netflix fell to a 52-week low on a light forward guide, and Taiwan Semiconductor fell more than 5% on a record quarter accompanied by a capital-spending increase. Blackbaud goes into that print having already run 36% off its late-June low.

Worse, it lands in the middle of the densest cluster of macroeconomic events of the year. The Federal Reserve meets on 28 and 29 July, and the largest technology companies report on 29 and 30 July, with their capital-spending plans being the market's main preoccupation. A $1.6B software company reporting into that window competes for attention with a rate decision and the artificial-intelligence capital-expenditure verdict on the same morning. Re-ratings that have to fight for oxygen tend to be muted or delayed; results landing in early August would have been cleaner.

The second hazard is the 2026 renewal cohort. This is the first large tranche of the three-year contracts Blackbaud began signing in 2023, and management stated on the 30 April 2025 call that renewals surge in the second quarter and the first part of the third. Retention has held at 92% to 93%; anything with an 8 in front of it re-prices this stock immediately and correctly, because retention is the entire moat.

The third hazard is the one nobody on any earnings call has asked about: leverage into a tightening Federal Reserve. Blackbaud carries about $1.19B of borrowings against $42M of its own cash — roughly 2.9 times earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation with stock compensation expensed, or about 3.6 times owner earnings. It drew $64.9M of new debt in the first quarter of 2026 while spending $82.1M on repurchases. The priced base case for this Federal Reserve is a rate rise by December, not a cut. If profits pause and borrowing costs rise together, the buyback is the adjustable item — and the buyback is the main structural bid under these shares. Note also that this thesis explicitly does not require rate cuts to work; it simply becomes harder if rates rise, which is the correct way round in the current regime.

The fourth is seasonal and easy to misread. The first quarter is Blackbaud's weakest cash quarter by a wide margin — $49.8M of free cash flow in the first quarter of 2026, and only $0.7M in the first quarter of 2025. Anyone extrapolating a single quarter's cash generation in either direction will get this badly wrong.
positioning_washout:
There was a forced-selling event in this stock, it was violent, and — critically for anyone underwriting it today — it is largely over.

The evidence for it is on the tape. On 18 June 2026 about 6.9 million shares changed hands, roughly ten times the surrounding daily average of about 640,000, with the stock near its 52-week low of $25.58. A single session at ten times normal volume, at the low, is the signature of price-insensitive selling — mandate-driven or index-driven — rather than considered fundamental exit. Supporting that reading: short interest rose 30.2% during March, to about 2.46 million shares or 5.5% of the float, and institutional holders were trimming through the period. The company has also fallen out of mid-capitalisation territory at a $1.6B market value, which mechanically hands it from one set of mandates to another — a one-way seller with no natural buyer at the same size.

There is no dividend here, so there is no yield-focused shareholder base to be flushed by a cut. The mechanical selling was about size and index membership, not income.

But the important half of this analysis is the timing, and it argues against acting now. From the late-June low the stock has recovered to $34.91 — up roughly 36% in five weeks, including 4.7% on Friday 24 July and a further 6.7% today on the Student First partnership announcement. Volume has been falling through the rally rather than rising. The forced sellers appear to be done. That means the marginal buyer from here is a discretionary investor who has to form a view on the artificial-intelligence displacement question, not a passive fund with no choice. The washout was the opportunity, and someone else has already harvested most of it. That is the single clearest reason this is a watchlist name today and would have been an entry six weeks ago.
moderator_conclusion:
My call is to put Blackbaud on the watchlist rather than buy it here, and the specific level I am waiting for is a return toward $27, which is where the adverse sum-of-the-parts case sits and roughly where the stock actually cleared six weeks ago.

Let me be clear about what I think is true, because most of it favours the bulls. The three loudest bearish signals on this company are all measurement artefacts. The revenue decline is a divestiture. The negative return on capital is a 2024 write-off year. The distress-zone solvency score is arithmetic on a book equity that a $1.42B buyback erased. Strip those out and you have a business with 92% to 93% customer retention, two-thirds of revenue under multi-year contract, gross margins expanding 160 basis points year over year, a perfect 9-out-of-9 quality-of-earnings score, earnings beats in five of six quarters, mid-teens returns on capital, and a share count that has fallen 10.3% in seven quarters net of all stock compensation. The supplied peer comparison calls this a value trap on the strength of two facts that are simply wrong, and I have corrected them rather than inherited them.

I also want to be clear that I am not marking this down because the catalyst is spent or because there is no dramatic event. The dated event here — the 29 July print — is real, and in this book a company's residual value case is judged on its own merits regardless of event heat. I have done that. My base sum-of-the-parts is about $44 a share against a market price of $34.91, which is a genuine discount of roughly a fifth.

So why not buy it? Two reasons, both about price and timing rather than about the business.

The first is that the opportunity has already been substantially taken. Five weeks ago this stock traded at $25.58 into a session of ten-times-normal volume — a mechanical, price-insensitive flush. Today it is $34.91, up 36% from that low, with 6.7% of it added this morning. The margin of safety has compressed from something like a third to about a fifth, and the buyer at this price is no longer picking up shares from a forced seller. Buying the wash-out is a strategy; buying the recovery from the wash-out at a 36% markup is a different and much worse one.

The second is that the immediate setup is genuinely poor. Blackbaud reports in two days having already warned that profits will dip this quarter to fund artificial-intelligence spending — and it reports into the same 48 hours as a Federal Reserve decision and the largest technology companies' capital-spending guidance. This is a tape that has been punishing exactly this message. The freshest analyst target on the Street, Stifel's $30.00 dated 10 July 2026, sits below today's price. Estimates are still being cut, not raised.

Against all of that sit two facts I cannot argue away. Insiders have made zero open-market purchases against seven sales, including the chief financial officer selling 9% of his direct holding within weeks of the low. And management is funding its buyback partly with borrowed money — $64.9M drawn against $82.1M repurchased in a single quarter — while carrying $1.19B of debt into a central bank whose base case is a rate rise, not a cut. Those two things together are why I hold the moat at narrow rather than wide and stop the conviction at moderate.

On the structural question — is generative artificial intelligence going to eat this business — my judgement is that the threat is material but not terminal, and therefore that the cheapness is mostly a fear-print rather than a melting base. Displacement announces itself through churn and price concessions, and neither is visible: retention is holding and gross margin is going up. Blackbaud's customers are structurally the least equipped buyers in the economy to migrate a system of record holding regulated donor and payment data. But I will not pretend the question is settled, and management's refusal to put a single dollar of artificial-intelligence revenue into any published forecast means the bull case there remains, for now, an assertion rather than a number.

The plan, then. Watch the 29 July print for one number above all others: renewal retention. If it holds at 92% to 93% and full-year guidance is reaffirmed, and the stock still gives back toward $27 in the macro noise of that week, this becomes a straightforward purchase with a $44 target and a believable path to more. If retention slips below 92%, the moat argument fails, the leverage stops being manageable, and I want nothing to do with it at any price.

**Prepared:** 27 July 2026 · **Price used:** $34.91 (NASDAQ, US dollars, live quote 27 July 2026; up 6.7% on the day from a $32.71 prior close) · **Market value:** about $1.60B · **Signal class:** deep value

The entry dated 29 October 2025 is **not Blackbaud** — it is Bausch + Lomb's third-quarter 2025 earnings call, spliced into the file by mistake. Everything in it (Miebo, contact lenses, intraocular lenses, Brent Saunders) belongs to a different company. I have discarded it entirely. The practical consequence is that I have **no Blackbaud third-quarter 2025 call**, so the narrative chain below runs Q1-2025 → Q2-2025 → *(gap)* → Q4-2025 → Q1-2026. I have filled the gap with the reported third-quarter numbers rather than management's words, and I flag it because a missing quarter is exactly where a story usually changes.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

Blackbaud sells the software that non-profits, private schools, universities, hospital foundations and corporate giving programmes use to raise and account for money — Raiser's Edge NXT for fundraising, Financial Edge NXT for accounting, YourCause for corporate employee giving. It has done so for about 45 years. Across the five usable quarters the story moves through three distinct phases.

**Phase one — "we are a Rule of 40 company" (first half of 2025).** The opening emphasis is operational self-improvement. Chief executive Mike Gianoni frames the business around the Rule of 40, a software-industry shorthand where revenue growth plus profit margin should sum to at least 40. In the first quarter of 2025 he reports "a Rule of 40 score of 40.1%" and calls it a milestone on the "journey to the Rule of 45 by 2030." By the second quarter he goes further: "we delivered a Rule of 45, our highest quarterly rule of performance in the company's history." The supporting drivers named are unglamorous and checkable — moving customers from one-year to three-year contracts, shutting company-owned data centres, renegotiating vendor contracts, writing off office leases, and buying back stock aggressively.

**Phase two — "we have a data moat" (February 2026).** The fourth-quarter 2025 call is where the equity story is deliberately re-founded. Gianoni opens by declaring the Rule of 40 goal "accomplished two years ahead of plan," then pivots hard to confront what he calls "the big question our industry is facing. Will AI be beneficial to system of record vertical software firms like Blackbaud or detrimental." His answer is a new central claim: "We have a data moat. - **Q1 2025 — assured, concrete, defensive-flavoured.** The dominant anxiety is federal grant funding to non-profit customers, and Gianoni answers it with a structural argument: "our solutions are not in the funds flow from federal agencies, but are used for fundraising from individual donors, which is even more critical now." - **Q4 2025 — a deliberate re-founding, and the first defensive note about the company's own industry.** Gianoni volunteers the existential question unprompted: "Will AI be beneficial to system of record vertical software firms like Blackbaud or detrimental." Management that raises the bear case itself is usually either confident or pre-empting. The tell is what follows: an unusually long, almost technical passage about data provenance, the "4 V's framework," identity resolution and licensed data sets. Length here signals effort, not ease — this is a claim being defended rather than demonstrated.
- **Q1 2026 — the tone narrows and hardens around one product.** Almost every confidence statement now routes through the Development Agent. The prepared remarks repeat the Q4 data-moat passage nearly verbatim, which suggests a message being held rather than developed.

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Score: High on what they commit to. The gap is what they refuse to commit to.**

The checkable promises were kept, and in one case beaten early:

- **The Rule of 40 target was hit two years ahead of schedule.** Promised over a multi-year horizon in early 2025, delivered by the end of that year.
- **The buyback was delivered to the letter.** Guided to 3%–5% of shares in 2025; by the first quarter they had already done "about 4.2%," and Tony Boor noted "about 15%. We've now purchased back just in the last year." The share count confirms it independently.

Excluding all artificial-intelligence revenue from both the 2026 guide and the 2030 aspiration, then repeatedly describing it as "the plus," is a deliberately low bar. Chief financial officer Chad Anderson did the same thing with the July 2025 tax legislation: "we think it will be meaningful and our intent will be to provide an update at the next call. **The credibility gap is the growth step-down.** "Mid-single-digit plus" in early 2025 became 4%–4.5% for 2026. Management never reconciled the two. An investor listening to the Q1 2025 call and the Q4 2025 call back to back would hear a lower number presented in the same confident register, with no acknowledgement that the bar moved.

## 5. Analyst pressure points

**The question management keeps not answering: what is artificial intelligence actually worth to you, in dollars?** Koji Ikeda of Bank of America pushed on it in Q1 2025 and got: "we have not separately charged for any of these separate capabilities." He pushed again in Q2 2025, asking specifically about standalone stock-keeping units and whether pricing would be fee-based or consumption-based. Gianoni opened with "I can spend an hour on that one," then declined: "I'm not going to preannounce that." By Q1 2026 there is finally a number — "tens of thousands per year" — but still no unit count, no bookings figure, no attach rate, and no contribution to guidance. Four consecutive calls of pressure have produced one price point and no revenue.

**The question that has already turned into bad news: renewals.** Ikeda asked about the 2026 renewal cohort in Q1 2025. Kirk Materne of Evercore ISI asked in Q2 2025 specifically about the first tranche of three-year deals coming back around "in the beginning of next year." Gianoni deflected both toward cross-selling: "we don't wait for the contract renewal. About half our sales team are focused on cross-selling anyway." In Q4 2025, Rob Oliver of Baird pressed on non-profit customer stress from federal and local funding cuts, citing "a bunch of survey work out there." That entire cluster of questions is now the central bear case — a Seeking Alpha piece dated 29 April 2026 is titled, precisely, "2026 Renewals Will Be The Major Test."

**What analysts worry about that management is not addressing.** Nobody on any of these calls asks the leverage question. With about $1.19B of borrowings against $42M of the company's own cash, and buybacks being partly funded with drawn debt, the interaction between a pausing profit line and a rising cost of debt is the single most under-examined risk on the page. Boor touched it once, glancingly, in Q1 2025 — "Debt is up a little bit, as you saw and interest expense is up a bit" — and no one followed up.

**One deflection worth naming.** In Q4 2025, Oliver addressed his non-profit-stress question directly to Gianoni, and Anderson — the chief financial officer — answered it instead, opening with "Yes, sure, Rob." The substance was fine. The handoff on the single most sensitive demand question of the call is a small thing, but it is the kind of small thing worth noticing.

---

## 6. Red flags and green flags

**Red flags**

- **Insiders sell, and only sell.** Zero open-market purchases against seven sales totalling 54,801 shares. Most pointedly, the chief financial officer sold 6,205 shares — 9% of his direct holding, cutting it from 69,074 to 62,869 — in a filing reported 8 June 2026, with the stock near $27 and within weeks of its low. That is the single most damaging fact in this file. Management's own words in Q1 2025 were that "Blackbaud continues to be a sound investment choice." Nobody inside acted on it.
- **Growth guided to the floor of their own band** (Q4 2025), one year into a five-year plan.
- **Profit growth pauses in the current quarter.** Management guided on the Q1 2026 call for adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation to decline slightly year over year in the second quarter, to fund artificial-intelligence investment. In a market that has been punishing exactly this — spending up, guidance soft — that is a poorly timed message.
- **Debt-funded repurchases.** $64.9M drawn against $82.1M bought back in Q1 2026.
- **Stock compensation of about $95M a year** flatters headline free cash flow by roughly a third.
- **The centrepiece of the story is in none of the numbers**, by management's own repeated statement.

**Green flags**

- **The buyback is real, large and verifiable** — 10.3% of the fully diluted share count retired in seven quarters, net of all stock compensation.
- **Quality of earnings is pristine.** A Piotroski score of 9 out of 9, the maximum, meaning every one of nine accounting-quality tests passes.
- **Margins are genuinely expanding** — gross margin up 160 basis points year over year in Q1 2026 — and returns on capital have recovered to roughly 15–16% from the 2024 impairment trough.
- **Retention of 92%–93%** on a base where roughly two-thirds of revenue now sits under three-year-or-longer contracts, and "more than 20% have asked to move to 4-year or longer" (Q4 2025).
- **Demand resilience has been stress-tested.** The response to the federal-funding scare is the best-argued passage in the file, and it is falsifiable: Blackbaud's software sits in the individual-donor fundraising flow, not the government grant flow. Management reports no customer failures.
- **A payments business inside the software.** Just over a third of revenue is transaction-based, growing high single digits organically, and structurally tied to the system of record.

---

## 7. Hidden signals

**"Data moat" appears from nowhere and immediately becomes the load-bearing phrase.** It is absent from both 2025 calls in this file. It arrives fully formed in February 2026 and is repeated near-verbatim in April 2026. A phrase that appears simultaneously in prepared remarks and press releases — Blackbaud's own 15 May 2026 release argues its products are "deeply embedded, difficult to replicate, and trusted to act" — is a message that has been through a communications process. That does not make it false. It does mean the company knows this is the question on which its multiple now depends.

**Blackbaud names Anthropic Claude as an internal engineering tool on two calls.** Gianoni cites "Microsoft GitHub Copilot and Anthropic Claude" for "code generation, software bug remediation and new product development," and says agents built in engineering have been "reducing workloads from days to hours." This is worth sitting with, because it cuts both ways: the same technology that lets Blackbaud produce software far more cheaply also lowers the cost for anyone who wants to build a competing donor database. Management presents only the first half of that trade.

**The competitive framing shifts from "market leader" to "system of record."** Early calls lean on scale and breadth. Later calls lean on position in the workflow — "you have to be sort of inside the system of record to be able to do that and we're the system of record, which is a pretty significant competitive advantage." That is a narrower, more defensive claim, and a more honest one.

**A new pricing vocabulary that has not yet been used.** Gianoni repeatedly signals that agent pricing might move to usage or outcome models — "we're looking at usage models and other models of pricing" — yet the first agent shipped on "an annual subscription fee... It's not usage-based yet." The gap between the pricing they describe and the pricing they charge is where the upside case lives or dies.

**The chief financial officer handover was clean and pre-signalled.** Boor moved to corporate development in April 2025 after 14 years, replaced by Anderson, a 12-year internal veteran and former chief accounting officer, with both men on the transition call. Twelve months later Anderson is answering demand questions directly. Orderly succession, no restatement, no auditor change — the boring outcome, which is the good one.

**Something mechanical happened to this stock in June 2026.** On 18 June 2026 about 6.9 million shares changed hands — roughly ten times the surrounding daily average — with the stock near its 52-week low of $25.58. Short interest had already risen 30.2% during March, to about 2.46 million shares or 5.5% of the float. A single day of volume at ten times normal, at the low, is the signature of price-insensitive selling: index or mandate-driven, not a considered fundamental exit. With the market value now around $1.6B, the company has also fallen out of mid-capitalisation territory, which hands it from one set of mandates to another.

---

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict (for the director)

**Trajectory classification: STABLE.** The earnings base is intact and improving in quality — margins expanding, returns on capital recovered to the mid-teens, cash conversion real, share count falling 6% a year. What is deteriorating is the growth rate, from mid-single-digit-plus to roughly 4%. What is being added is optionality that management refuses to put a number on. Those roughly cancel. This is not a company falling apart; it is a company whose compounding rate stepped down a gear while its multiple stepped down three.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing.** Not the valuation, and not the artificial-intelligence question — it is **the interaction between leverage and the pause in profit growth, timed against a rising cost of debt.** Blackbaud carries about $1.19B of borrowings against $42M of its own cash — roughly 2.9 times earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation once stock compensation is properly expensed, or about 3.6 times owner earnings. It is funding its buyback partly with new borrowings. It has guided profits to dip in the current quarter. And it is doing this into a Federal Reserve whose priced base case is a rate rise by December. Every one of those facts is individually manageable. Together they mean the buyback — which is the main structural bid under this stock and the main reason per-share value compounds at all — is the thing that gets cut if anything goes wrong. Size for that, not for the cheap headline multiple.

**Economic moat: NARROW, and stable rather than widening.** The moat type is **switching costs**, reinforced by a genuine **intangible data asset**. The switching-cost claim is evidenced, not asserted: 92%–93% retention, roughly two-thirds of revenue under three-year-or-longer contracts, and a customer base — small non-profits and private schools — that management accurately describes as having "limited IT resources" and high staff turnover, which is precisely the customer least able to execute a migration. The data claim is weaker: real, but "cannot be commoditized" is a statement of hope about a technology whose entire history is commoditisation.

I judge it **narrow rather than wide** for one reason: 92%–93% retention means 7%–8% of the base leaves every year, and the company must grow through that headwind. A wide-moat franchise does not lose a fourteenth of its customers annually. On width *trend*, the prompt's own test — rising returns and expanding margins point to widening — would argue for improvement, and gross margin up 160 basis points with returns recovering to the mid-teens does satisfy it mechanically. I decline to call it widening, because the margin gain is being produced by data-centre closures, offshoring to India and internal automation rather than by pricing power, and because a franchise with genuinely strengthening competitive position does not simultaneously guide growth down to the floor of its own range. **Stable** is the honest read.

**Secular threat: MATERIAL, not terminal.** The relevant force is generative-artificial-intelligence displacement of software whose moat is workflow habit. The bear case is easy to state: agents make it dramatically cheaper to build a donor database, and Blackbaud's own engineering commentary is evidence for it. But three things argue against terminal impairment. First, the buyer is structurally the least equipped in the economy to self-build or migrate. Second, the product is a system of record holding sensitive donor and payment data under compliance obligations — the hardest category of software to displace, because the switching cost is regulatory and reputational, not just technical. Third, and most concretely, the margins are going the wrong way for a displacement story: gross margin is expanding and retention is holding at 92%–93%. Displacement shows up as churn and price concessions first, and neither is visible yet.

**So is the cheapness a fear-print or a value trap?** Predominantly a **fear-print, with a real and unresolved question attached.** The three loudest bear signals on the screen — negative returns on capital, shrinking revenue, and a distress-zone solvency score — are all measurement artefacts, of a 2024 write-off, a divestiture, and a buyback respectively. Strip them out and the business earns mid-teens returns, converts a quarter of revenue to cash, and retires a tenth of its shares every eighteen months. That is not a melting ice cube. But the growth deceleration is genuine, the leverage is genuine, and the insiders have voted with seven sales and no purchases. The discount is earned in part — just far less of it than the screen implies.

There is no solvency question here; there is a leverage question, which is different and which I take seriously below.

Where the Street is right and the bulls are wrong, and this is why I am not more aggressive: growth genuinely is decelerating. Guidance moved from mid-single-digit-plus in early 2025 to roughly 4% to 4.5% for 2026, the floor of the company's own 4% to 6% long-term band in year one. And management has excluded every dollar of artificial-intelligence revenue from every published figure — the 2026 guide and the 2030 targets alike — which means the entire narrative centrepiece of the last four earnings calls is unfalsifiable. An investor cannot check it, and neither can I.

So the disagreement is real but bounded. The market is pricing a melting franchise; the evidence says a slow-growing, cash-generative one with a genuine unresolved question about its long-term defensibility. That gap is worth roughly the difference between $34.91 and $44 — not the difference between $34.91 and the old $74.88 high.

valley_of_death:
The risky window here is unusually short and unusually specific: it starts in two days.

The first hazard is the second-quarter print on 29 July 2026, and the problem is not the result — it is the setup. Management has already told the market that adjusted profits will decline slightly year over year this quarter to fund artificial-intelligence investment. Spending up and margins pausing is precisely the message that the current tape has been punishing: in the same reporting season Netflix fell to a 52-week low on a light forward guide, and Taiwan Semiconductor fell more than 5% on a record quarter accompanied by a capital-spending increase. Blackbaud goes into that print having already run 36% off its late-June low.

Worse, it lands in the middle of the densest cluster of macroeconomic events of the year. The Federal Reserve meets on 28 and 29 July, and the largest technology companies report on 29 and 30 July, with their capital-spending plans being the market's main preoccupation. A $1.6B software company reporting into that window competes for attention with a rate decision and the artificial-intelligence capital-expenditure verdict on the same morning. Re-ratings that have to fight for oxygen tend to be muted or delayed; results landing in early August would have been cleaner.

The second hazard is the 2026 renewal cohort. This is the first large tranche of the three-year contracts Blackbaud began signing in 2023, and management stated on the 30 April 2025 call that renewals surge in the second quarter and the first part of the third. Retention has held at 92% to 93%; anything with an 8 in front of it re-prices this stock immediately and correctly, because retention is the entire moat.

The third hazard is the one nobody on any earnings call has asked about: leverage into a tightening Federal Reserve. Blackbaud carries about $1.19B of borrowings against $42M of its own cash — roughly 2.9 times earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation with stock compensation expensed, or about 3.6 times owner earnings. It drew $64.9M of new debt in the first quarter of 2026 while spending $82.1M on repurchases. The priced base case for this Federal Reserve is a rate rise by December, not a cut. If profits pause and borrowing costs rise together, the buyback is the adjustable item — and the buyback is the main structural bid under these shares. Note also that this thesis explicitly does not require rate cuts to work; it simply becomes harder if rates rise, which is the correct way round in the current regime.

The fourth is seasonal and easy to misread. The first quarter is Blackbaud's weakest cash quarter by a wide margin — $49.8M of free cash flow in the first quarter of 2026, and only $0.7M in the first quarter of 2025. Anyone extrapolating a single quarter's cash generation in either direction will get this badly wrong.

There was a forced-selling event in this stock, it was violent, and — critically for anyone underwriting it today — it is largely over.

The evidence for it is on the tape. On 18 June 2026 about 6.9 million shares changed hands, roughly ten times the surrounding daily average of about 640,000, with the stock near its 52-week low of $25.58. A single session at ten times normal volume, at the low, is the signature of price-insensitive selling — mandate-driven or index-driven — rather than considered fundamental exit. Supporting that reading: short interest rose 30.2% during March, to about 2.46 million shares or 5.5% of the float, and institutional holders were trimming through the period. The company has also fallen out of mid-capitalisation territory at a $1.6B market value, which mechanically hands it from one set of mandates to another — a one-way seller with no natural buyer at the same size.

There is no dividend here, so there is no yield-focused shareholder base to be flushed by a cut. The mechanical selling was about size and index membership, not income.

But the important half of this analysis is the timing, and it argues against acting now. From the late-June low the stock has recovered to $34.91 — up roughly 36% in five weeks, including 4.7% on Friday 24 July and a further 6.7% today on the Student First partnership announcement. Volume has been falling through the rally rather than rising. The forced sellers appear to be done. That means the marginal buyer from here is a discretionary investor who has to form a view on the artificial-intelligence displacement question, not a passive fund with no choice. The washout was the opportunity, and someone else has already harvested most of it. That is the single clearest reason this is a watchlist name today and would have been an entry six weeks ago.
moderator_conclusion:
My call is to put Blackbaud on the watchlist rather than buy it here, and the specific level I am waiting for is a return toward $27, which is where the adverse sum-of-the-parts case sits and roughly where the stock actually cleared six weeks ago.

Let me be clear about what I think is true, because most of it favours the bulls. The three loudest bearish signals on this company are all measurement artefacts. The revenue decline is a divestiture. The negative return on capital is a 2024 write-off year. The distress-zone solvency score is arithmetic on a book equity that a $1.42B buyback erased. Strip those out and you have a business with 92% to 93% customer retention, two-thirds of revenue under multi-year contract, gross margins expanding 160 basis points year over year, a perfect 9-out-of-9 quality-of-earnings score, earnings beats in five of six quarters, mid-teens returns on capital, and a share count that has fallen 10.3% in seven quarters net of all stock compensation. The supplied peer comparison calls this a value trap on the strength of two facts that are simply wrong, and I have corrected them rather than inherited them.

I also want to be clear that I am not marking this down because the catalyst is spent or because there is no dramatic event. The dated event here — the 29 July print — is real, and in this book a company's residual value case is judged on its own merits regardless of event heat. I have done that. My base sum-of-the-parts is about $44 a share against a market price of $34.91, which is a genuine discount of roughly a fifth.

So why not buy it? Two reasons, both about price and timing rather than about the business.

The first is that the opportunity has already been substantially taken. Five weeks ago this stock traded at $25.58 into a session of ten-times-normal volume — a mechanical, price-insensitive flush. Today it is $34.91, up 36% from that low, with 6.7% of it added this morning. The margin of safety has compressed from something like a third to about a fifth, and the buyer at this price is no longer picking up shares from a forced seller. Buying the wash-out is a strategy; buying the recovery from the wash-out at a 36% markup is a different and much worse one.

The second is that the immediate setup is genuinely poor. Blackbaud reports in two days having already warned that profits will dip this quarter to fund artificial-intelligence spending — and it reports into the same 48 hours as a Federal Reserve decision and the largest technology companies' capital-spending guidance. This is a tape that has been punishing exactly this message. The freshest analyst target on the Street, Stifel's $30.00 dated 10 July 2026, sits below today's price. Estimates are still being cut, not raised.

Against all of that sit two facts I cannot argue away. Insiders have made zero open-market purchases against seven sales, including the chief financial officer selling 9% of his direct holding within weeks of the low. And management is funding its buyback partly with borrowed money — $64.9M drawn against $82.1M repurchased in a single quarter — while carrying $1.19B of debt into a central bank whose base case is a rate rise, not a cut. Those two things together are why I hold the moat at narrow rather than wide and stop the conviction at moderate.

On the structural question — is generative artificial intelligence going to eat this business — my judgement is that the threat is material but not terminal, and therefore that the cheapness is mostly a fear-print rather than a melting base. Displacement announces itself through churn and price concessions, and neither is visible: retention is holding and gross margin is going up. Blackbaud's customers are structurally the least equipped buyers in the economy to migrate a system of record holding regulated donor and payment data. But I will not pretend the question is settled, and management's refusal to put a single dollar of artificial-intelligence revenue into any published forecast means the bull case there remains, for now, an assertion rather than a number.

The plan, then. Watch the 29 July print for one number above all others: renewal retention. If it holds at 92% to 93% and full-year guidance is reaffirmed, and the stock still gives back toward $27 in the macro noise of that week, this becomes a straightforward purchase with a $44 target and a believable path to more. If retention slips below 92%, the moat argument fails, the leverage stops being manageable, and I want nothing to do with it at any price.

interrogator_dossier:
# Forensic Dossier — Blackbaud, Inc. (BLKB)

**Prepared:** 27 July 2026 · **Price used:** $34.91 (NASDAQ, US dollars, live quote 27 July 2026; up 6.7% on the day from a $32.71 prior close) · **Market value:** about $1.60B · **Signal class:** deep value

**A note on the source material before anything else.** The transcript bundle supplied for this name contains four calls dated 30 April 2025, 30 July 2025, 29 October 2025 and 10 February 2026, plus a fifth dated 29 April 2026. The entry dated 29 October 2025 is **not Blackbaud** — it is Bausch + Lomb's third-quarter 2025 earnings call, spliced into the file by mistake. Everything in it (Miebo, contact lenses, intraocular lenses, Brent Saunders) belongs to a different company. I have discarded it entirely. The practical consequence is that I have **no Blackbaud third-quarter 2025 call**, so the narrative chain below runs Q1-2025 → Q2-2025 → *(gap)* → Q4-2025 → Q1-2026. I have filled the gap with the reported third-quarter numbers rather than management's words, and I flag it because a missing quarter is exactly where a story usually changes.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

Blackbaud sells the software that non-profits, private schools, universities, hospital foundations and corporate giving programmes use to raise and account for money — Raiser's Edge NXT for fundraising, Financial Edge NXT for accounting, YourCause for corporate employee giving. It has done so for about 45 years. Across the five usable quarters the story moves through three distinct phases.

**Phase one — "we are a Rule of 40 company" (first half of 2025).** The opening emphasis is operational self-improvement. Chief executive Mike Gianoni frames the business around the Rule of 40, a software-industry shorthand where revenue growth plus profit margin should sum to at least 40. In the first quarter of 2025 he reports "a Rule of 40 score of 40.1%" and calls it a milestone on the "journey to the Rule of 45 by 2030." By the second quarter he goes further: "we delivered a Rule of 45, our highest quarterly rule of performance in the company's history." The supporting drivers named are unglamorous and checkable — moving customers from one-year to three-year contracts, shutting company-owned data centres, renegotiating vendor contracts, writing off office leases, and buying back stock aggressively.

**Phase two — "we have a data moat" (February 2026).** The fourth-quarter 2025 call is where the equity story is deliberately re-founded. Gianoni opens by declaring the Rule of 40 goal "accomplished two years ahead of plan," then pivots hard to confront what he calls "the big question our industry is facing. Will AI be beneficial to system of record vertical software firms like Blackbaud or detrimental." His answer is a new central claim: "We have a data moat. We have the most robust philanthropic data processed and gleaned in real time... This cannot be commoditized." Alongside it he introduces a new product category, Agents for Good, and a formal capital framework running to 2030 — organic revenue growth of 4% to 6% a year, double-digit earnings-per-share growth, and half of free cash flow committed to buying back stock.

**Phase three — "the agent is a new revenue line" (April 2026).** The first-quarter 2026 call reports that the Fundraising Development Agent "launched into general availability ahead of schedule." Gianoni gives it real commercial specificity for the first time: "we expect the price will be in the tens of thousands per year, and we expect to cross-sell subscriptions to thousands of existing customers." He also widens the addressable-market argument in an interesting way — arguing the agents can be sold out of customers' *staffing* budgets rather than their information-technology budgets, because a virtual fundraiser substitutes for a hire.

**What got quietly dropped.** In the first quarter of 2025 the guidance language was "mid-single-digit plus organic revenue growth." By February 2026 the long-term commitment had become "4% to 6%," and the 2026 guidance itself landed at roughly 4% to 4.5%. That is a genuine step down, delivered without ever being named as one. The word "plus" did a lot of work in the earlier framing; management now attaches it explicitly to the artificial-intelligence products instead — "we always say plus... well, that's where the plus comes from."

**What got added and never quantified.** Every single call from July 2025 onward is dominated by artificial intelligence. Yet in February 2026 Gianoni is unambiguous that none of it is in the numbers: "we do not have in those long-term numbers, our new AI products represented. It's just too early... it's not included in the '26 guide or the long-term aspirational." Repeated in April 2026: "we're still early stages of broader commercialization, which we view as potential upside over time." So the entire narrative centrepiece of the last four calls sits outside every figure the company has published. That is the defining tension in this name.

---

## 2. Claims versus financials (forensic)

I tested management's four biggest claims against the reported statements. Two hold up cleanly, one holds with a caveat, and one is contradicted by the company's own guidance.

| Management claim | Where said | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Rule of 40... accomplished two years ahead of plan" | Q4 2025 | Trailing-twelve-month revenue $1.139B; free cash flow $292M, a 25.6% margin; adjusted profit margins in the mid-30s. Growth plus margin clears 40 on the company's own definition. | **Holds** |
| Buyback discipline — "buying between 3% to 5% of our outstanding shares in 2025," later half of free cash flow through 2030 | Q1 2025, Q4 2025 | Fully diluted share count fell from 51.68M (Q2 2024) to 46.35M (Q1 2026) — down 10.3% in seven quarters, 6.3% in the last year alone. $82.1M repurchased in Q1 2026 alone. | **Holds — and over-delivers** |
| Margin expansion from data-centre closure, offshoring and internal AI use | Q4 2025, Q1 2026 | Gross margin 59.2% in Q1 2026 versus 57.6% a year earlier, up 160 basis points. Operating income $51.4M versus $20.4M. Returns on invested capital recovered to roughly 15–16% on trailing earnings. | **Holds** |
| "Mid-single-digit plus organic revenue growth" | Q1 2025 | 2026 guidance is roughly 4%–4.5%; Q1 2026 revenue of $281.1M was up 3.9% year over year. That is the bottom of their own long-term 4%–6% band in the first year of the plan. | **Contradicted by their own guide** |

**Three screener inputs on this name are wrong, and they matter.** The scan and the peer-comparison note both treat Blackbaud as a shrinking, capital-destroying, near-insolvent business. All three of those readings are artefacts:

- **"Revenue shrinking 2.3%."** That compares fiscal 2025 ($1.128B) to fiscal 2024 ($1.155B) — a decline caused by divesting EVERFI, not by the base eroding. Management flagged the distortion directly in Q2 2025: "This improvement would have been even higher had we adjusted for EVERFI." Organic growth was 5.8% in Q1 2025 and 6.8% in Q2 2025. The base is growing, just slowly.
- **"Return on invested capital of −1.2%."** That is fiscal 2024, the year Blackbaud took roughly $408M of impairment and other charges and reported a $283M net loss. On the trailing twelve months the company earned about $231M of operating profit on roughly $1.18B of invested capital — call it 15–16%. The negative figure describes a write-off, not the business.
- **"Altman-Z of 1.2," the so-called distress zone.** That score leans on book equity, and Blackbaud's book equity is $34.6M — a rounding error — purely because it has parked $1.42B of its own repurchased stock in the treasury account. Buying back a tenth of your shares mechanically erases book equity. Interest expense of about $67M a year is covered roughly 4.7 times by earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation. This is not a solvency signal.

**Where the numbers are genuinely poorer than the story.** Two places. First, free cash flow is flattered by stock-based compensation, which the cash-flow statement adds back: about $95M over the last twelve months, roughly a third of the $292M of reported free cash flow and 8.3% of revenue. Charge it as the real cost it is and owner earnings are closer to **$197M**, or about $4.28 a share. To be fair to management, they are paying for that dilution in cash — the share count is still falling — but an investor should anchor on $197M, not $292M. Second, **the buybacks are partly debt-funded**. In Q1 2026 the company drew $64.9M of new borrowings and spent $82.1M on repurchases. That is a levered-buyback machine, and it works only for as long as earnings hold.

---

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Rating: Stable, with the confidence relocating from the financials to the product roadmap.**

- **Q1 2025 — assured, concrete, defensive-flavoured.** The dominant anxiety is federal grant funding to non-profit customers, and Gianoni answers it with a structural argument: "our solutions are not in the funds flow from federal agencies, but are used for fundraising from individual donors, which is even more critical now." Confidence is grounded in retention: "retentions still in the 92, 93 percentile."
- **Q2 2025 — the peak.** "Our highest quarterly rule of performance in the company's history." Specific named customer wins (Cal Poly, SunnyBrook Foundation, Nasdaq, Chevron, Tyson Foods). This is the most offensive-toned call in the set.
- **Q4 2025 — a deliberate re-founding, and the first defensive note about the company's own industry.** Gianoni volunteers the existential question unprompted: "Will AI be beneficial to system of record vertical software firms like Blackbaud or detrimental." Management that raises the bear case itself is usually either confident or pre-empting. The tell is what follows: an unusually long, almost technical passage about data provenance, the "4 V's framework," identity resolution and licensed data sets. Length here signals effort, not ease — this is a claim being defended rather than demonstrated.
- **Q1 2026 — the tone narrows and hardens around one product.** Almost every confidence statement now routes through the Development Agent. The prepared remarks repeat the Q4 data-moat passage nearly verbatim, which suggests a message being held rather than developed.

**The shift from offence to efficiency is real but partial.** The margin story is increasingly built on cost levers with a shelf life — closing "the last 2" data centres, and what Gianoni openly calls "a natural labor arbitrage" from expanding the Blackbaud India office and moving away from third-party contractors. Those are one-time gains dressed as a trend. Set against that, the growth levers named are genuine and repeatable: price escalators inside multi-year contracts, cross-selling, and a transactional payments business running at "high single digits organically."

---

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Score: High on what they commit to. The gap is what they refuse to commit to.**

The checkable promises were kept, and in one case beaten early:

- **The Rule of 40 target was hit two years ahead of schedule.** Promised over a multi-year horizon in early 2025, delivered by the end of that year.
- **The buyback was delivered to the letter.** Guided to 3%–5% of shares in 2025; by the first quarter they had already done "about 4.2%," and Tony Boor noted "about 15%. We've now purchased back just in the last year." The share count confirms it independently.
- **The earnings record is strong.** The screener records beats in five of the last six quarters (83%). The most recent print, first-quarter 2026, beat on both lines — non-GAAP earnings of $1.14 a share against a $1.08 consensus compiled by Zacks, on revenue that also came in ahead.

There is a mild but recognisable **sandbagging pattern**, and management is nearly explicit about it. Excluding all artificial-intelligence revenue from both the 2026 guide and the 2030 aspiration, then repeatedly describing it as "the plus," is a deliberately low bar. Chief financial officer Chad Anderson did the same thing with the July 2025 tax legislation: "we think it will be meaningful and our intent will be to provide an update at the next call. But I would remind everyone that we've not included the potential impact into the revised guidance."

**The credibility gap is the growth step-down.** "Mid-single-digit plus" in early 2025 became 4%–4.5% for 2026. Management never reconciled the two. An investor listening to the Q1 2025 call and the Q4 2025 call back to back would hear a lower number presented in the same confident register, with no acknowledgement that the bar moved.

**And the market has stopped extending credit.** Analyst price targets tell the story of a thesis being abandoned in stages: an average of $52.50 across eight targets over the past year, $41.67 across three in the last quarter, and a single $30.00 target from Stifel's Parker Lane on 10 July 2026 — cut from $45.00, itself cut from $50.00, itself cut from $70.00. Target velocity is running at −21% against the year-ago average. **The freshest target on the Street sits below today's $34.91 price.**

---

## 5. Analyst pressure points

**The question management keeps not answering: what is artificial intelligence actually worth to you, in dollars?** Koji Ikeda of Bank of America pushed on it in Q1 2025 and got: "we have not separately charged for any of these separate capabilities." He pushed again in Q2 2025, asking specifically about standalone stock-keeping units and whether pricing would be fee-based or consumption-based. Gianoni opened with "I can spend an hour on that one," then declined: "I'm not going to preannounce that." By Q1 2026 there is finally a number — "tens of thousands per year" — but still no unit count, no bookings figure, no attach rate, and no contribution to guidance. Four consecutive calls of pressure have produced one price point and no revenue.

**The question that has already turned into bad news: renewals.** Ikeda asked about the 2026 renewal cohort in Q1 2025. Kirk Materne of Evercore ISI asked in Q2 2025 specifically about the first tranche of three-year deals coming back around "in the beginning of next year." Gianoni deflected both toward cross-selling: "we don't wait for the contract renewal. About half our sales team are focused on cross-selling anyway." In Q4 2025, Rob Oliver of Baird pressed on non-profit customer stress from federal and local funding cuts, citing "a bunch of survey work out there." That entire cluster of questions is now the central bear case — a Seeking Alpha piece dated 29 April 2026 is titled, precisely, "2026 Renewals Will Be The Major Test."

**What analysts worry about that management is not addressing.** Nobody on any of these calls asks the leverage question. With about $1.19B of borrowings against $42M of the company's own cash, and buybacks being partly funded with drawn debt, the interaction between a pausing profit line and a rising cost of debt is the single most under-examined risk on the page. ## 7. Hidden signals

**"Data moat" appears from nowhere and immediately becomes the load-bearing phrase.** It is absent from both 2025 calls in this file. It arrives fully formed in February 2026 and is repeated near-verbatim in April 2026. A phrase that appears simultaneously in prepared remarks and press releases — Blackbaud's own 15 May 2026 release argues its products are "deeply embedded, difficult to replicate, and trusted to act" — is a message that has been through a communications process. That does not make it false. It does mean the company knows this is the question on which its multiple now depends.

**Blackbaud names Anthropic Claude as an internal engineering tool on two calls.** Gianoni cites "Microsoft GitHub Copilot and Anthropic Claude" for "code generation, software bug remediation and new product development," and says agents built in engineering have been "reducing workloads from days to hours." This is worth sitting with, because it cuts both ways: the same technology that lets Blackbaud produce software far more cheaply also lowers the cost for anyone who wants to build a competing donor database. Management presents only the first half of that trade.

**The competitive framing shifts from "market leader" to "system of record."** Early calls lean on scale and breadth. Later calls lean on position in the workflow — "you have to be sort of inside the system of record to be able to do that and we're the system of record, which is a pretty significant competitive advantage." That is a narrower, more defensive claim, and a more honest one.

**A new pricing vocabulary that has not yet been used.** Gianoni repeatedly signals that agent pricing might move to usage or outcome models — "we're looking at usage models and other models of pricing" — yet the first agent shipped on "an annual subscription fee... It's not usage-based yet." The gap between the pricing they describe and the pricing they charge is where the upside case lives or dies.

**The chief financial officer handover was clean and pre-signalled.** Boor moved to corporate development in April 2025 after 14 years, replaced by Anderson, a 12-year internal veteran and former chief accounting officer, with both men on the transition call. Twelve months later Anderson is answering demand questions directly. Orderly succession, no restatement, no auditor change — the boring outcome, which is the good one.

**Something mechanical happened to this stock in June 2026.** On 18 June 2026 about 6.9 million shares changed hands — roughly ten times the surrounding daily average — with the stock near its 52-week low of $25.58. Short interest had already risen 30.2% during March, to about 2.46 million shares or 5.5% of the float. A single day of volume at ten times normal, at the low, is the signature of price-insensitive selling: index or mandate-driven, not a considered fundamental exit. With the market value now around $1.6B, the company has also fallen out of mid-capitalisation territory, which hands it from one set of mandates to another.

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict (for the director)

**Trajectory classification: STABLE.** The earnings base is intact and improving in quality — margins expanding, returns on capital recovered to the mid-teens, cash conversion real, share count falling 6% a year. What is deteriorating is the growth rate, from mid-single-digit-plus to roughly 4%. What is being added is optionality that management refuses to put a number on. Those roughly cancel. This is not a company falling apart; it is a company whose compounding rate stepped down a gear while its multiple stepped down three.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing.** Not the valuation, and not the artificial-intelligence question — it is **the interaction between leverage and the pause in profit growth, timed against a rising cost of debt.** Blackbaud carries about $1.19B of borrowings against $42M of its own cash — roughly 2.9 times earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation once stock compensation is properly expensed, or about 3.6 times owner earnings. It is funding its buyback partly with new borrowings. It has guided profits to dip in the current quarter. And it is doing this into a Federal Reserve whose priced base case is a rate rise by December. Every one of those facts is individually manageable. Together they mean the buyback — which is the main structural bid under this stock and the main reason per-share value compounds at all — is the thing that gets cut if anything goes wrong. Size for that, not for the cheap headline multiple.

**Economic moat: NARROW, and stable rather than widening.** The moat type is **switching costs**, reinforced by a genuine **intangible data asset**. The switching-cost claim is evidenced, not asserted: 92%–93% retention, roughly two-thirds of revenue under three-year-or-longer contracts, and a customer base — small non-profits and private schools — that management accurately describes as having "limited IT resources" and high staff turnover, which is precisely the customer least able to execute a migration. The data claim is weaker: real, but "cannot be commoditized" is a statement of hope about a technology whose entire history is commoditisation.

I judge it **narrow rather than wide** for one reason: 92%–93% retention means 7%–8% of the base leaves every year, and the company must grow through that headwind. A wide-moat franchise does not lose a fourteenth of its customers annually. On width *trend*, the prompt's own test — rising returns and expanding margins point to widening — would argue for improvement, and gross margin up 160 basis points with returns recovering to the mid-teens does satisfy it mechanically. I decline to call it widening, because the margin gain is being produced by data-centre closures, offshoring to India and internal automation rather than by pricing power, and because a franchise with genuinely strengthening competitive position does not simultaneously guide growth down to the floor of its own range. **Stable** is the honest read.

**Secular threat: MATERIAL, not terminal.** The relevant force is generative-artificial-intelligence displacement of software whose moat is workflow habit. The bear case is easy to state: agents make it dramatically cheaper to build a donor database, and Blackbaud's own engineering commentary is evidence for it. But three things argue against terminal impairment. First, the buyer is structurally the least equipped in the economy to self-build or migrate. Second, the product is a system of record holding sensitive donor and payment data under compliance obligations — the hardest category of software to displace, because the switching cost is regulatory and reputational, not just technical. Third, and most concretely, the margins are going the wrong way for a displacement story: gross margin is expanding and retention is holding at 92%–93%. Displacement shows up as churn and price concessions first, and neither is visible yet.

**So is the cheapness a fear-print or a value trap?** Predominantly a **fear-print, with a real and unresolved question attached.** The three loudest bear signals on the screen — negative returns on capital, shrinking revenue, and a distress-zone solvency score — are all measurement artefacts, of a 2024 write-off, a divestiture, and a buyback respectively. Strip them out and the business earns mid-teens returns, converts a quarter of revenue to cash, and retires a tenth of its shares every eighteen months. That is not a melting ice cube. But the growth deceleration is genuine, the leverage is genuine, and the insiders have voted with seven sales and no purchases. The discount is earned in part — just far less of it than the screen implies.
